title: Distributed Job Scheduler
subtitle: Designing a cloud-scale cron & delayed task execution engine with time-bucketed sharding, hierarchical timing wheels, and fencing-token leases
keyTakeaways: Partition schedule scanning by `(time_bucket_minute, shard_id)` so schedule Pollers perform sequential partition scans on the current minute window rather than expensive unindexed range queries across billions of future jobs.

Bridge the gap between minute-level DB buckets and sub-second execution accuracy using an in-memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel (`HashedWheelTimer`) before dispatching ready tasks to Kafka worker queues.

Guarantee safe execution under worker crashes using Lease Expirations (`visibility_timeout`), Heartbeat extensions, and monotonically increasing `fencing_token` numbers so zombie workers cannot corrupt downstream state.

sections.heading: 1. Requirement Gathering
sections.body: A distributed job scheduler (like AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Google Cloud Tasks, or Temporal/Quartz at scale) allows thousands of internal microservices and external tenants to schedule one-off delayed tasks, recurring cron jobs, and multi-step DAG workflows.
bullets: Functional — One-Time & Recurring Cron Jobs: Schedule one-off delayed executions (`run_at = now + 2h`) or recurring cron schedules (`0 */6 * * *`) with timezone awareness.

Functional — Configurable Retries & Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ): Support exponential backoff with jitter (`initial=1s, factor=2.0, max_attempts=5`) and route permanently failed executions to a tenant DLQ.

Functional — Job Cancellation, Pause & Status Inspection: Allow tenants to cancel or pause a job prior to execution and query historical execution logs (`QUEUED`, `RUNNING`, `SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`, `TIMED_OUT`).
Functional — Lease Heartbeats & DAG Chaining: Support long-running jobs via periodic worker heartbeats and trigger child jobs upon parent completion.
Non-Functional — High Timing Precision: P99 dispatch lag (difference between scheduled `next_run_at` and actual push to worker queue) < 500 milliseconds.

Non-Functional — At-Least-Once Execution with Safe Idempotency: 99.99% availability; zero dropped executions (`at-least-once` delivery) paired with fencing tokens and idempotency keys to achieve `effectively-once` side effects.
Out of Scope: Building the container hypervisor/Kubernetes kubelet itself (workers execute HTTP webhooks, gRPC calls, or pre-registered serverless task handlers).

sections.heading: 2. Scale Assumption
sections.body: We size the platform for a multi-tenant cloud infrastructure provider scheduling billing cycles, reminder notifications, ETL pipelines, and cache warmers.
bullets: Total Registered Active Jobs: 500 Million active recurring/delayed job definitions across 100,000 tenant accounts.
Daily Job Executions: 10 Billion job executions triggered per day.

Read:Write Ratio: Each job execution produces ~4 state writes (`SCHEDULED` -> `DISPATCHED` -> `RUNNING` -> `SUCCEEDED` + next cron slot insertion) and ~2 status/poll reads (~1:2 read-to-write ratio, heavily write-intensive).
Peak Traffic Multiplier: 5x spike at top-of-the-hour (`00:00`) and top-of-the-minute boundaries because humans overwhelmingly write cron expressions like `0 * * * *` or `0 0 * * *`.
Payload Sizes: Job definition metadata = 1 KB; Schedule bucket index entry = 128 bytes; Execution history record = 512 bytes.

sections.heading: 3. Capacity Estimation (QPS, Memory, 5-Year Storage & Bandwidth)
sections.body: The defining challenge of a job scheduler is the **Top-of-the-Hour Cron Spike**: millions of recurring jobs fire at `XX:00:00`, requiring smooth pre-fetching into memory wheels and partitioned queue buffers.
bullets: Execution Trigger QPS: 10 Billion executions / 86,400s = ~115,740 executions/sec average -> 578,700 executions/sec at 5x top-of-the-hour burst.
Database State Mutation Write QPS: 115,740 executions/sec * 4 state transitions = ~463,000 writes/sec average (batched via Kafka and asynchronous bulk upserts).

Timing Wheel & Lease Cache Memory (RAM): Pre-fetching 2 minutes of upcoming executions at peak (578,700/sec * 120s = ~69.4M upcoming tasks) * 256 bytes per wheel slot entry = ~17.8 GB RAM distributed across 64 Poller coordinator nodes (~280 MB per node).

5-Year Storage (Job Metadata + Execution Audit History): 500M active jobs * 1 KB = 500 GB. Execution logs = 10B/day * 512 B = 5.12 TB/day. Retention policy: keep hot in CockroachDB/Cassandra for 14 days (71.7 TB), and archive compressed (5:1 Zstd) to S3 for 5 years (1.02 TB/day * 1,825 days = 1.86 PB).
Network Bandwidth: Dispatch Ingress/Egress = 578,700 peak tasks/sec * 1 KB payload = ~578 MB/sec peak across the Kafka and Worker fleet.

sections.heading: 4. API Design & Entities (with Entity Diagram)
sections.body: Core external REST/gRPC/WebSocket API contracts, request/response payloads, and underlying storage entities with primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), secondary/clustering indexes (IDX), and relationship cardinalities.
bullets: POST /api/v1/jobs — Registers a one-off delayed task or recurring cron job and writes the next due slot into (minute_bucket, shard_id).
POST /internal/v1/executions/{executionId}/heartbeat — Worker renews lease_expires_at every 15s using its fencing_token.
POST /internal/v1/executions/{executionId}/complete — Marks execution SUCCEEDED and schedules the next cron occurrence.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Box Diagram
sections.body: The architecture decouples **Schedule Discovery** (Poller nodes scanning time-bucketed shards and loading a `HashedWheelTimer`) from **Task Execution** (stateless Worker pools consuming prioritized Kafka topics and maintaining leases).
bullets: Shard Coordinator (Etcd / ZooKeeper): Assigns the 256 logical `shardId`s across the 64 active Poller nodes using ephemeral leases. If Poller Node 7 crashes, its 4 shards are immediately reassigned to surviving Poller nodes within 3 seconds.

Two-Tier Time Resolution (Minute Bucket DB + In-Memory HashedWheelTimer): The database only groups jobs by `minute_bucket` (`epoch_ms / 60000`). A Poller queries all tasks in `(current_minute, shard_id)` once every few seconds and loads them into a Netty `HashedWheelTimer` (512 ticks, 100ms resolution) to fire each task at its exact millisecond timestamp.
Priority Kafka Queues: Prevents noisy-neighbor batch jobs from delaying latency-sensitive user reminders by splitting topics into `tasks-p0-realtime`, `tasks-p1-standard`, and `tasks-p2-batch`.

Lease Reaper & Retry Engine: Background scanner that detects `RUNNING` executions whose `leaseExpiresAt < NOW()`, increments `fencingToken`, and schedules an exponential backoff retry or moves the job to the Dead-Letter Queue.

sections.heading: 6. Deep Dive Flows (Flow 1 & Flow 2)
sections.body: Let us trace: (1) Partitioned Minute-Bucket Polling into an In-Memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel, and (2) Worker Lease Acquisition, Heartbeat Extension, Zombie Fencing, and Next Cron Slot Calculation.
bullets: Flow 1 (Time-Bucket Polling + Timing Wheel Dispatch): Instead of running `SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= NOW()` across 500M rows, a Poller node responsible for `shardId = 42` queries `WHERE minute_bucket = 29841200 AND shard_id = 42 AND claimed = false LIMIT 5000`. It marks them claimed, inserts `JobExecution` rows with `fencingToken = attemptNo`, and schedules each task inside an in-memory `HashedWheelTimer` for `delay = nextRunAtMs - System.currentTimeMillis()`. When the wheel tick fires, the task is published to Kafka.

Flow 2 (Worker Lease, Zombie Fencing & Cron Roll-Forward): When Worker A pulls the task from Kafka, it sets `status = RUNNING` and `leaseExpiresAt = NOW() + 30s`, renewing it every 10s. If Worker A suffers a 45-second JVM stop-the-world GC pause, its lease expires. The Lease Reaper marks attempt 1 `TIMED_OUT` and spawns attempt 2 with `fencingToken = 2` on Worker B. When Worker A wakes up from GC and tries to call the downstream service or mark its execution complete, the downstream service and scheduler DB reject `fencingToken = 1 < 2`.

sections.heading: 7. Further Improvements & Production Readiness
sections.body: To survive top-of-the-hour cron thundering herds and noisy multi-tenant workloads, production schedulers layer in jitter, quotas, and DAG state machines.
bullets: Deterministic Cron Smearing (Fuzzy Cron): When tenants register `@hourly` or `0 0 * * *` jobs that do not require exact-second wall-clock precision, hash the `jobId` to add a deterministic offset `hash(jobId) % 60` seconds, smoothing the midnight spike by 60x.

Per-Tenant Token Bucket Quotas & Fair Queuing: Enforce per-tenant concurrency limits in Redis so a single tenant scheduling 5 million backfill webhooks at 12:00 PM cannot starve other tenants' P0 payment jobs.

Downstream Circuit Breaking (Adaptive Backpressure): If a tenant's target webhook endpoint starts returning HTTP 503/429s, automatically trip a per-endpoint circuit breaker and pause dispatching slots for that endpoint rather than saturating worker threads on connection timeouts.

Old Minute-Bucket Partition Drop (`DROP PARTITION`): Because `schedule_slots` is range-partitioned by `minute_bucket`, completed minute partitions older than 2 hours can be dropped via an $O(1)$ metadata operation rather than expensive row-by-row `DELETE` vacuuming.

Multi-Region Active-Passive / Active-Active Failover: Replicate `JobDefinition` and `ScheduleSlot` across regions via CockroachDB/Spanner so if `us-east-1` loses power, `us-west-2` Pollers immediately claim the orphaned shards.

tradeOffs.option: Time-Bucketed Sharded DB (`minute_bucket, shard_id`) + In-Memory Timing Wheel
tradeOffs.pros: Durable across node crashes, scales linearly by adding shard IDs, avoids massive DB index scans, and delivers sub-100ms precision via `HashedWheelTimer`.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires two-stage handoff (DB poll every few seconds into in-memory wheel, then push to Kafka).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Cloud-scale distributed schedulers with 100M+ jobs and strict durability guarantees.

tradeOffs.pros: Ultra-fast sub-millisecond `ZRANGEBYSCORE` polling and simple implementation.
tradeOffs.cons: RAM-bound for 500M+ large job payloads, and Redis asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged jobs during a primary node crash.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Medium-scale delayed message queues (< 20M active tasks) where occasional failover loss is acceptable.

tradeOffs.option: Single Relational Table with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
tradeOffs.pros: Zero external coordination (no Etcd/ZooKeeper or Timing Wheel needed); ACID simplicity.
tradeOffs.cons: B-Tree index bloat and MVCC vacuuming bottleneck severely above ~10,000 executions/sec.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic or departmental job queues (< 5,000 QPS).

interviewTip: When designing a Distributed Job Scheduler, explicitly explain why `SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at <= NOW()` fails at scale (unbounded index scan contention + MVCC dead-tuple churn) and show how composite partitioning by `(minute_bucket, shard_id)` paired with an in-memory `HashedWheelTimer` and `fencing_token` leases solves scalability, precision, and zombie workers simultaneously.
